title: The UK Is a Country Made of Countries
beats: Fires three naming questions (UK? England? Great Britain?) then zooms from world to continent to the islands.
UK shown as a purple region: a country of four countries; England in red, why it gets confused with the whole.
Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland each get a color; mutual stereotypes as comic glue; all are British citizens.
Full name reveals Great Britain; switches axis: geographical vs political term.
'GB = England+Scotland+Wales' is mostly but not completely true: offshore islands listed.
Ireland is also a geographic term holding two countries; Republic of Ireland vs Northern Ireland.
Review: two islands, five countries, which four form the UK.
New puzzle: why is British royalty on Canadian money? Opens the Empire layer.
The Crown as a one-man corporation; God delegates power to avoid micromanagement.
Commonwealth Realm defined and listed by population.
Crown Dependencies: not independent, local autonomy, UK can overrule.
'Are we done now?' Gibraltar and Falklands as loose threads; Overseas Territories, formerly Crown Colonies.
Final Venn diagram nests UK, British Isles, Crown, Dependencies, Realm, Territories.

metrics.misconception: yes: UK = England = Great Britain; Ireland as a country
metrics.examples: 5 countries -> 2 islands -> 15 realms -> 3 dependencies -> 16 territories; scope widens from home island to globe
metrics.ending: Single Venn diagram recap of all categories

principles.1: confirmed: 0:00 starts from the names the viewer already confuses and a world map zoom.
principles.2: confirmed: each new category gets exactly one color/region, no extra symbols (0:18-1:07).
principles.3: partly: color code reused throughout, but the final Venn (4:43) is a new interface introduced only at the end.
principles.4: partly: one analogy (Crown as one-man corporation, 2:47), not used as a ramp to rigor.
principles.7: not-observed: definitions are told, not discovered.
principles.8: partly: idea rate spikes in rapid lists (3:20, 4:26) treated as skimmable; dense nested-axis content gets a review pause at 1:58.
principles.9: partly: the 'geographic vs political' distinction repeated for Great Britain (1:07) and Ireland (1:40).
principles.10: confirmed: one country -> four -> islands -> empire -> global territories.
principles.11: confirmed: political/geographic split before Crown; Crown before Realm/Dependencies/Territories.
principles.12: partly: Canada money, EU, Falklands war link to outside knowledge.
principles.13: partly: kid-simple coloring, but little 'why' for tool choice; caveat on GB at 1:24 shows expert precision.

new_moves.name: new:axis-switch
new_moves.what: Reveals confusion comes from mixing two classification axes (geographic vs political) and labels each term by axis
new_moves.evidence: 1:07 Great Britain is geographical not political; 1:40 same for Ireland

new_moves.name: new:list-as-texture
new_moves.what: Long exhaustive lists read fast as texture, signalling 'you need not memorize these'

new_moves.name: new:are-we-done-yet
new_moves.what: Rhetorical stop-check that reopens with loose threads, keeping momentum across categories

theory: Grey dissolves a vocabulary muddle by assigning every term a fixed color and a single axis (geographic vs political vs Crown), then nesting them outward from the viewer's home in rings. The final Venn diagram is the payoff: the entire video was building one picture, and the recap is that picture.
velocity: Scene builder: give each new term a persistent color/region and never repurpose it; build toward one final composite diagram.
Orchestrator: when a learner confuses terms, diagnose which classification axes are being mixed and teach the axis first.
Voice: deliver exhaustive lists at speed with on-screen highlights and an explicit cue that they are reference, not to memorize.
Learner model: insert a mini-recap after each nested layer (as at 1:58) before opening the next ring.
Evals: test whether learner can place a new item (e.g. Bermuda) into the final Venn, not recite definitions.
quote: the United Kingdom is not a single country, but... a country of countries
